analysis.one_liner: Lets the Labor Department fine health plans that shortchange mental health and addiction coverage.
analysis.headline: The bill, giving the Labor Department power to penalize plans that violate mental health parity rules, was introduced in September 2022 and died in the Senate committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law already requires group health plans to cover mental health and substance use treatment no more restrictively than physical health care. But the Labor Department has had limited power to punish plans that break this rule. This bill would let the Department impose civil monetary penalties on plans, their sponsors, and their administrators that fail to provide equal mental health coverage.
analysis.who_benefits: People with employer-sponsored health insurance who need mental health or substance use disorder treatment, since plans would face real financial consequences for limiting that care more tightly than physical health care.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People needing mental health or addiction treatment

how_it_helps.text: The bill gives the Department of Labor authority to enforce the parity requirements for group health plans covering mental health and substance use disorder benefits [S2].
It adds civil monetary penalties for any plan sponsor or administrator that fails to meet the mental health and substance use disorder parity requirements [S3].
It carves out an exception so the Labor Department can enforce this rule directly, instead of leaving participants to sue on their own [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and the employers who sponsor group health plans, who would face federal fines for parity violations, with any penalty costs potentially passed through to premiums.

drawbacks.text: Fines on plans and their employer sponsors raise compliance costs, and large employers warn that such costs are often passed into premiums paid partly by workers themselves.
The bill adds only an enforcement tool; it does not change or clarify the parity standards themselves, so disputes over what counts as a violation would continue.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is meaningful but narrow: mental health parity has been law for years, and the main gap is enforcement, so fines could make existing rights real for people with employer coverage. The cost is higher compliance and possible premium pressure on employers and workers. On balance a targeted fix, though it does nothing for people whose plans' parity violations rest on unclear rules.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate health committee in September 2022, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Sen. Christopher Murphy introduced the bill on September 8, 2022, with Sen. Tina Smith and Sen. Ben Ray Luján as original cosponsors [S3].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day [S5].
No further action was taken: no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote before the 117th Congress ended [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and large employers that sponsor health plans are better off, because they face no federal fines for mental health parity violations. People relying on mental health coverage gained nothing.

for.name: Sen. Christopher Murphy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Parity Enforcement Act of 2022 and led its push in the Senate.

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.role: Senate committee with jurisdiction over the bill
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on September 8, 2022 and took no further action before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors were Democrats, but no member or group ever voted on or publicly opposed the bill, so no partisan split appears in the record.

industries.note: The bill would expose insurers to Labor Department civil monetary penalties when their group plans cover mental health or substance use care less generously than physical care. That cost is the mechanism for enforcing coverage people are already owed.
Employers who sponsor or administer group plans could face penalties, and may see compliance costs passed into premiums. Workers at those firms are the same people the bill's enforcement protects.
